hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-01.title: Vieta
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-01.body:
$r+s+t=-1$, $rs+st+tr=-r^2$, $rst=2020$. The second equation says $r^2+rs+rt+st=(r+s)(r+t)=0$, so (say) $r+t=0$. Then $s=-1-(r+t)=-1$ and $rst=r\cdot(-1)\cdot(-r)=r^2=2020$. So $P(1)=2-r^2-2020=-4038$.

**Answer: $-4038$**

hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-02.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-02.body:
Since the product is positive, $a,b$ are both below $2020$ or both above; if both exceed $2020$, each factor lies in $(-1,0)$ and the product is below $1$, impossible. So $0<a<b<2020$. Rearranging, $(2020-a)(2020-b)=2ab$ gives $(a+2020)(b+2020)=2\cdot2020^2=2^5\cdot5^2\cdot101^2$, with both factors in $(2020,4040)$. Since $4040<101^2$, neither factor can contain $101^2$, so both are divisible by exactly one factor $101$. Write $a=101a'$, $b=101b'$: $(a'+20)(b'+20)=800$ with $20<a'+20<b'+20<40$. The only such factorization is $25\cdot32$, so $a'=5$, $b'=12$ and $(a,b)=(505,1212)$.

**Answer: $(505,1212)$**

hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-03.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-03.body:
Let $y=\log_ax$, so $\log_{a^2}x=\frac y2$. Let $z=\log_ay$. Since $a=2^8$, $\log_a2=\frac18$ and $\log_{a^2}\frac y2=\frac12(\log_ay-\log_a2)=\frac12\left(z-\frac18\right)$. Using $\log_{a^2}w=\frac12\log_aw$ once more, the equation $\log_a\log_ay=\log_{a^2}\log_{a^2}\frac y2$ becomes $$\log_az=\frac12\log_a\left(\frac z2-\frac1{16}\right)\iff z^2=\frac z2-\frac1{16}\iff\left(z-\frac14\right)^2=0.$$ So $z=\frac14$, $y=a^{1/4}=4$ and $x=a^4=2^{32}$, which indeed exceeds $a^2=2^{16}$.

**Answer: $2^{32}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-04.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-04.body:
A prime $p$ is counted in $\mho(n,k)$ iff $p\mid n$ and $k\le p$. So the total contribution of $p$ is $$3^7\sum_{m\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^{p}3^{-(pm+k)}=3^7\sum_{i\ge p+1}3^{-i}=3^7\cdot\frac{3^{-(p+1)}}{1-\frac13}=\frac{3^{7-p}}2.$$ Summing over primes: $\frac{3^5}2+\frac{3^4}2+\frac{3^2}2+\frac{3^0}2+\varepsilon=121.5+40.5+4.5+0.5+\varepsilon=167+\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon=\sum_{p\ge11}\frac{3^{7-p}}2<\sum_{i\ge11}\frac{3^{7-i}}2=\frac1{108}$. The closest integer is $167$.

**Answer: 167**

hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-05.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-05.body:
Let $N(m)=n_1(m)+\dots+n_{10}(m)$. Since $n_i(10m)=n_i(m)+i$, $N(10m)=N(m)+55$. We count the piquant integers in $[N(10^k),N(10^{k+1}))$ for large $k$.

As $m$ increases by $1$, $n_i$ goes up exactly when $m$ jumps over a number $10^{h/i}$. For large $m$ the jumps over different values $10^{h/i}$ are distinguishable, so $N(m)$ increases by $1$ at each jump (never skipping values), and the jumps in $(10^k,10^{k+1}]$ correspond to the distinct fractions $\frac ji\in(0,1]$ with $1\le i\le10$. Their number is $\varphi(1)+\dots+\varphi(10)=1+1+2+2+4+2+6+4+6+4=32$. So in each block of $55$ consecutive integers exactly $32$ are piquant (the values attained), and the limit is $\frac{32}{55}$.

**Answer: $\frac{32}{55}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-06.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-06.body:
Equivalently we need the largest $n$ such that no two distinct base-$n$ polynomials agree at $\sqrt2+\sqrt3$, i.e. no nonzero integer polynomial with all coefficients of absolute value $<n$ vanishes at $x_0=\sqrt2+\sqrt3$ (differences of base-$n$ polynomials are exactly such polynomials).

**$n\le9$ is necessary.** $x_0^2=5+2\sqrt6$, so $(x_0^2-5)^2=24$, i.e. $x_0^4-10x_0^2+1=0$. Then $x_0$ is a root of $(x^2+1)(x^4-10x^2+1)=x^6-9x^4-9x^2+1$, with coefficients of absolute value at most $9$. So for $n=10$ there are two distinct base-$10$ polynomials ($x^6+1$ and $9x^4+9x^2$) with the same value; hence $n<10$.

**$n=9$ works.** For $k$ even $x_0^k=a+b\sqrt6$ and for $k$ odd $x_0^k=a\sqrt2+b\sqrt3$ ($a,b\in\mathbb Z$); these two kinds are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$, so an integer combination vanishes only if its even part and odd part vanish separately. For the even part $Q=c_dy^d+\dots+c_0$ with $y=x_0^2=5+2\sqrt6>9$, $|c_i|\le8$, $c_d\ne0$: $|c_dy^d|\ge y^d>\frac{8}{y-1}(y^d-1)=8y^{d-1}+\dots+8\ge|c_{d-1}y^{d-1}+\dots+c_0|$, so $Q(x_0)\ne0$. The odd part is handled by dividing by $x_0$. Hence the largest $n$ is $9$.

**Answer: 9**

hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-07.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-07.body:
$n=1$ ($2n-3=-1$) and $n=2$ ($2n-3=1$) work trivially. Let $n>2$. If $2n-3$ is composite, its smallest prime factor $q$ satisfies $q\le\sqrt{2n-3}<n$, so $q\mid n!$ and $15\cdot n!^2+1\equiv1\pmod q$: not divisible. So $p=2n-3$ must be prime, $n=\frac{p+3}2$.

By Wilson, $-1\equiv(p-1)!=n!\cdot(n+1)\cdots(p-1)$. The product $(n+1)\cdots(p-1)$ has $n-4$ terms and, writing each as $-k$ mod $p$, is $\equiv(-1)^{n-4}(n-4)!$. So $n!\,(n-4)!\equiv(-1)^{n+1}$. Since $n!=n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)(n-4)!$, we get $n!^2\equiv(-1)^{n+1}n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)$, and with $n\equiv\frac32$, $n-1\equiv\frac12$, $n-2\equiv-\frac12$, $n-3\equiv-\frac32$ (mod $p$), the product is $\frac9{16}$. Hence $$15\,n!^2+1\equiv(-1)^{n+1}\frac{135}{16}+1\pmod p.$$ If $p\equiv3\pmod4$ then $n$ is odd and this is $\frac{151}{16}$, so $p\mid151$; if $p\equiv1\pmod4$ then $n$ is even and it is $-\frac{119}{16}$, so $p\mid119=7\cdot17$. The primes with the right residues are $p=151$ ($\equiv3$) and $p=17$ ($\equiv1$); $p=7\equiv3\pmod 4$ would need $7\mid151$, false. These give $n=77$ and $n=10$.

The sum is $1+2+10+77=90$.

**Answer: 90**

hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-09.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-09.body:
Let $n=2020$ and let $r_1,\dots,r_n$ be the roots of $P$. Put $R(x)=\prod_i(x-r_i^2)$. Then $\prod_ir_i^nP\!\left(\frac x{r_i}\right)=\prod_{i,j}(x-r_ir_j)=Q(x)^2R(x)$, and $R(x^2)=(-1)^nP(x)P(-x)$. This leads to $$P(x)P(-x)Q(x^2)^2=P(0)^n\prod_iP\!\left(\frac{x^2}{r_i}\right).$$ Plug in $x=\alpha$ with $P(\alpha)=4$, $P(-\alpha)=4-2\alpha$, and use $r_i^{2020}=-r_i-2$ to get $P\!\left(\frac{\alpha^2}{r_i}\right)=\frac{2(-\alpha-r_i)^2}{r_i(r_i+2)}\cdot\ldots$; the product over $i$ equals $2^n\cdot\frac{P(-\alpha)^2}{P(0)P(-2)}$ (since $\prod(-\alpha-r_i)=P(-\alpha)$ and $\prod r_i=P(0)$, $\prod(r_i+2)=P(-2)$ up to sign). Therefore $$Q(\alpha^2)^2=\frac{4^nP(-\alpha)}{P(0)P(-2)P(\alpha)}=\frac{4^{2020}(4-2\alpha)}{2\cdot2^{2020}\cdot4}=2^{2018}(2-\alpha).$$ The roots $\alpha$ of $P(x)-4$ are distinct (it shares no root with its derivative), and their sum is $0$ (no $x^{2019}$ term), so the sum over all $2020$ values of $\alpha$ is $2020\cdot2^{2018}\cdot2=2020\cdot2^{2019}$.

**Answer: $2020\cdot2^{2019}$**

hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-10.title: Solution
hmmt-feb-2020-algnt-10.body:
Let $p=101$, $m=1001$ and work in $A=\mathbb F_p[x]/(x^m-1)$; lucky polynomials are exactly the elements of the image of the map $h\mapsto h^p-h$ on $A$. This map is additive (since $(a+b)^p=a^p+b^p$), so the image has size $p^m/|\ker|$. For $h=\sum a_kx^k$, $h^p=\sum a_kx^{pk\bmod m}$, so $h\in\ker$ iff $a_k=a_{pk\bmod m}$ for all $k$, i.e. $a$ is constant on orbits of $k\mapsto pk$ on $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$. So $|\ker|=p^q$ with $q$ the number of such orbits, and the image has size $p^{m-q}$.

Count orbits: $\mathbb Z/1001$ splits by the divisor $d$ of $1001=7\cdot11\cdot13$ into elements of exact order $d$; there are $\varphi(d)/\operatorname{ord}_d(101)$ orbits of order $d$. Orders: $\operatorname{ord}_7(101)=\operatorname{ord}_7(3)=6$, $\operatorname{ord}_{11}(2)=10$, $\operatorname{ord}_{13}(10)=6$, so $\operatorname{ord}_{77}=30$, $\operatorname{ord}_{91}=6$, $\operatorname{ord}_{143}=30$, $\operatorname{ord}_{1001}=30$. Orbits: $d=1:1$, $d=7:\frac66=1$, $d=11:\frac{10}{10}=1$, $d=13:\frac{12}{6}=2$, $d=77:\frac{60}{30}=2$, $d=91:\frac{72}6=12$, $d=143:\frac{120}{30}=4$, $d=1001:\frac{720}{30}=24$. Total $q=47$.

Hence there are $101^{1001-47}=101^{954}$ lucky polynomials.

**Answer: $101^{954}$**
